1058.title: Hatikvah
1058.howItsDone: Hatikvah is sung at state ceremonies in Israel and at Jewish community events, school graduations and gatherings in other countries, often with the audience standing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, each link, and your line, receives, and passes on. Did you tell a family story to someone new? Today, a song about the thing that gets handed on when there's little else to hold. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

A valley full of bones, very dry. That is the scene the prophet Ezekiel describes. In his vision, God tells him the bones are the whole house of Israel, and tells him what the people are saying, a sentence of despair. Our bones are dried up, they say, and "our hope is lost". In Hebrew, those last words are avdah tikvatenu: lost is our hope. Keep that phrase in your ear. Long after Ezekiel, a poem was written that answers it almost word for word. The poem became a song, and the song became a national anthem. Its name is a single Hebrew word. That word is today's word.
screen: `A VALLEY OF DRY BONES.` → `OUR HOPE IS LOST.` → `A POEM ANSWERS BACK.`

segments.voice: Hatikvah. Ha means the, and tikvah means hope: the hope. It is Israel's national anthem, and it is often sung at Jewish gatherings in other countries too. The words are short. In plain English, they go something like this: as long as, deep in the heart, a Jewish soul still yearns, and an eye still looks forward to the east, toward Zion, our hope is not yet lost, the hope of two thousand years: to be a free people in our land, the land of Zion and Jerusalem. Now listen for Ezekiel. The bones said avdah tikvatenu, our hope is lost. The anthem sings od lo avdah tikvatenu, our hope is not yet lost. Two small words, od lo, not yet, turn a sentence of despair around. And Ezekiel's vision does the same. Before those words of despair are even quoted, the bones have already come together and breath has entered them, and right after them, God promises to open the graves and bring the people home to the land of Israel. Notice what kind of hope the anthem sings. It isn't a victory song about something already won. It's a hope still being held, with the heart and with the eyes, facing a direction. The year has met this kind of hope before: in prayers that faced Jerusalem, in exile after exile, in people who kept saying next year. People hear the anthem differently, too. Israel has citizens who are not Jewish, and some of them have said a song about a Jewish soul doesn't speak for them; that conversation is part of Israel's life. But the word at the center of the song is one the Bible and the anthem share. Today's line is that word: the hope.
screen: `HA, THE. TIKVAH, HOPE.` · `A SOUL YEARNS, AN EYE LOOKS TO ZION.` · `OUR HOPE IS NOT YET LOST.` · `A HOPE STILL HELD, NOT A VICTORY SONG.` · then, large: `THE HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: name one hope. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Find one hope you've been carrying for a while. Not a wish for a thing, but a hope: for a person, a place, a change that hasn't come yet. Say it to yourself in a few plain words. Then put the anthem's two small words in front of it: not yet. Not yet lost. Let it sit there, still unfinished, still held. If you pray, you can bring that hope before God in your own words. If you don't, simply keep it company until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Hatikvah. The hope: Israel's anthem, which answers the dry bones' our hope is lost with our hope is not yet lost. Today's word.
Your line: the hope. Today, when something feels lost, try adding two words to the sentence: not yet. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: From generation to generation
1059.hook: the phrase that ends the Kedushah
1059.howItsDone: When a minyan is present, the leader repeats the Amidah aloud and the congregation joins in the Kedushah, standing; in the Ashkenazi wording the leader then continues with l'dor vador nagid godlecha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hatikvah, and your line: the hope. Did you put not yet in front of something that felt lost? Today, a phrase the synagogue sings to keep hope and memory moving. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

Partway through a weekday service, the leader begins to repeat the standing prayer, the Amidah, out loud, and the room changes. The leader and the congregation start trading lines from the Bible, back and forth, a call and an answer. Some people rise up onto their toes. First comes Isaiah's vision of the angels: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". Then Ezekiel's: blessed be the glory of the LORD from His place. Then a verse from the Psalms. And just before the closing hallelujah, the congregation sings today's word.
screen: `THE AMIDAH, REPEATED ALOUD.` → `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` → `JUST BEFORE HALLELUJAH.`

segments.voice: L'dor vador. Dor means generation. L'dor, to a generation; vador, and a generation. From generation to generation. That section of the service is the Kedushah, the prayer of holiness, and its last verse is from Psalm 146: the LORD will reign for ever, your God, O Zion, l'dor vador, hallelujah. Then, in the Ashkenazi wording, the leader picks the phrase straight back up and carries on: l'dor vador nagid godlecha, from generation to generation we will tell of your greatness. Look at the shape of it. Isaiah's angels call holy in heaven. Ezekiel hears the glory moving from its place. And then the prayer comes down to earth and lands on something very human: parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren. In this prayer, holiness isn't only sung. It's handed down. The phrase has roots in the Torah too. At the burning bush, God gives Moses a name and says, "this is My memorial unto all generations". In Hebrew, l'dor dor. A memorial is a thing that keeps memory alive, so the zachor of a few days ago and today's phrase belong together: remembering is how anything gets from one generation to another. And notice that the Kedushah is a conversation. The congregation answers the leader; the leader answers the congregation. Passing something on works like that too. The young don't only receive. They answer back, with questions and new melodies of their own, and the answer becomes part of what the next generation hears. Today's line: generation to generation.
screen: `DOR: A GENERATION.` · `THE KEDUSHAH ENDS: L'DOR VADOR.` · `THIS IS MY MEMORIAL UNTO ALL GENERATIONS.` · `A CALL, AND AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `GENERATION TO GENERATION.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: connect with a younger person. Let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone younger than you: a child, a niece or nephew, a student, a new coworker, a neighbor's kid. Hold their face for a moment. Ask yourself two things. What do I know that they might need someday? And what do they know that I don't? Both count. Then choose one small way to reach them this week: a message, a question, a story, a skill. If you pray, you can say the psalm's two words quietly: l'dor vador. If you don't, just hold their name. The bell holds the time.
L'dor vador. From generation to generation: the words near the end of the Kedushah, from Psalm 146. Today's word.
Your line: generation to generation. Today, ask someone younger what they're into, and really listen to the answer. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: What history teaches
1060.tomorrow: Year three close: the people and their story
1060.howItsDone: Jews return to their history in the yearly cycle of fasts and festivals, at the Seder, on memorial days and in study, and the phrase am Yisrael chai, the people of Israel lives, is sung at gatherings of different kinds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, l'dor vador, and your line: generation to generation. Did you ask someone younger a real question, and listen? Today, before the year closes, a question for the whole of it. Day one thousand sixty.

History doesn't hand out lessons by itself. People draw them, and they don't always draw the same ones. The same hard years can teach one family to hold on tighter and another to start over somewhere new. So today isn't a verdict on the Jewish story. It's a look at a few threads that keep turning up in it, through kings and exiles, study halls and new countries, and the Shoah, which the year approached with care. Five of them, and one sentence that holds them together.
screen: `HISTORY DOESN'T HAND OUT LESSONS.` → `PEOPLE DRAW THEM.` → `FIVE THREADS, ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: What history teaches. The first two belong together: surviving and remembering. Again and again this year, the people outlived the powers that tried to end them, and they did it partly by refusing to forget. Zachor. A yahrzeit candle on the right date. A story told to the children. The third is adapting. When the Temple was about to fall, the Talmud tells that Yochanan ben Zakkai was carried out of besieged Jerusalem and asked the Roman commander for one thing: Yavneh and its sages. A place to keep teaching. With the altar gone, Jewish life was rebuilt around study, prayer and the family table. The form changed so the heart could stay. The fourth is arguing. The houses of Hillel and Shammai argued for so long that the Talmud tells of a voice from heaven settling it. It said that both, these and these, are the words of the living God, and that the law follows Hillel, in part because Hillel's students were gentle and put the other side's words before their own. Argument, in this story, isn't a crack in the tradition. It's part of how the tradition lives. And the fifth is hoping. Prayers that faced Jerusalem. Next year. Od lo avdah tikvatenu, our hope is not yet lost. None of these five is a victory lap. This year did not pretend the story was all triumph. But put them side by side and they spell out today's line, a sentence that is sometimes sung as a song, am Yisrael chai, the people of Israel lives. Or, as today's line puts it plainly: we are still here.
screen: `SURVIVING, AND REMEMBERING.` · `ADAPTING: YAVNEH AND ITS SAGES.` · `ARGUING: THESE AND THESE.` · `HOPING: NOT YET LOST.` · then, large: `WE ARE STILL HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: list three lessons. If you have paper, take it. If not, use your fingers to count. Let your breath slow. Look back over this year's story, or over your own family's history, or both. What has it taught you? Not what it's supposed to teach. What it actually taught you. Find three things, in a few words each. One might be about losing something. One might be about starting again. One might surprise you. Hold all three at once. If you pray, you can give thanks for the people who carried the story this far. The bell holds the time.
Yavneh. The place Yochanan ben Zakkai asked for as Jerusalem fell, where Jewish life was rebuilt around study, prayer and the family table. Today's word.
Your line: we are still here. Today, share one of your three lessons with someone, and ask them for one of theirs. Day one thousand sixty.

1061.title: Year three close: the people and their story
1061.hook: from Joshua's river to today, one long story
1061.tomorrow: Year four opens: how it all works
1061.howItsDone: Jews say the Shehecheyanu blessing at the start of festivals, on first times and at milestones, and they retell their history in the cycle of festivals and fasts, from Passover to Tisha b'Av to Hanukkah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yavneh, and your line: we are still here. Did you trade one lesson with someone? Today is the last day of year three. Day one thousand sixty-one.

Back near the start of this year, the people crossed the Jordan, and Joshua set up stones on the far bank. They weren't there to be admired. They were there to be asked about, so that someday the children would say, "What mean ye by these stones?" and someone would have to tell the story. A year later, the same question can be put to the whole year. What were all those days for? Kings and prophets, poems and exiles, rabbis and refugees, a language woken up, a people still singing. Today, one answer, told as one story.
screen: `STONES ON THE FAR BANK.` → `WHAT MEAN YE BY THESE STONES?` → `ONE ANSWER, ONE STORY.`

segments.voice: Year three close. Here is the year, as the answer to the children's question. First, the Former Prophets. The day Moses died, the story didn't stop. Joshua crossed the river, the judges rose and fell, Samuel anointed kings, and the kingdom split and fell. Second, the Latter Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve, voices that warned before the fall and comforted after it, down to Ezekiel's dry bones standing up again. Third, the Writings: Ruth choosing a people, Job arguing with heaven, Esther finding her voice, Lamentations weeping over the city, Ezra and Nehemiah coming home to rebuild. And then the Bible's last page turned, and the story kept going. The Maccabees and Rome. Yavneh and the Talmud. Babylon and Baghdad, Spain and the Rhineland, Safed and the villages of the east. The Americas, the return of Hebrew, the Shoah, and after. Women whose names were nearly lost. And Jewish life today, with its food and music and arguments and candles. That's the year: a people and their story. Not a list of dates, but one long thread, picked up by each generation and handed on. And notice where the Tanakh itself chooses to stop. The Torah ends on the bank of the Jordan, with the land in sight and the crossing still ahead. The Prophets open with the command to cross. The story is built to keep going past its own pages. Which is why the stones on the bank were never a monument to a finished event. They were a question waiting for the next child. Today's line: the story goes on.
screen: `THE FORMER PROPHETS: A RIVER, KINGS.` · `THE LATTER PROPHETS: WARNING, COMFORT.` · `THE WRITINGS, THEN AFTER THE BIBLE.` · `A QUESTION WAITING FOR THE NEXT CHILD.` · then, large: `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: say a blessing for the story. Sit, and let your breath slow. Let the year pass in front of you: one story that stayed with you, one person, one line. When Jews reach a new season or a milestone, there is a blessing they say, the Shehecheyanu. In English it blesses God, who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season. If you pray, you can say it now, in Hebrew or in English, for the year you've just walked. If you don't, simply sit with the thought that you've arrived here, at the end of a long story and the start of the next part. The bell holds the time.
Shehecheyanu. Hebrew for who has kept us alive: the blessing for milestones, fitting for a year that carried the people's whole story to the river's edge and beyond. Today's word.

Your line: the story goes on. Today, tell someone one story from this year, the way a parent answers a child who asks about the stones. Tomorrow, year four, and how it all works. Day one thousand sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 1061 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR FOUR OPENS: HOW IT ALL WORKS.`

1062.title: Year four opens: how it all works
1062.hook: three years of story, text and history; now the machinery: law, thought, streams, character, language
1062.howItsDone: Jewish study often runs in a cycle, returning to the same texts year after year, and learners are encouraged to bring their own questions to the text, often with a study partner.

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three closed, with stones on the far bank of the Jordan, and your line: the story goes on. Who did you tell one story to? Today, year four begins. Day one thousand sixty-two.

A watch lies face down on a repair bench. For years its owner only ever saw the front: two hands going round, the hours passing. Then the jeweler pries off the back, and there it is. Tiny wheels with teeth. A spring wound tight. Something rocking back and forth, steady as breath. Nothing about the time has changed. The watch tells the same hours it always told. But now you can see why it keeps going. That is where this path stands this morning. Three years of the front of the watch: stories, the text, a people's history. This year, the back comes off.
screen: `A WATCH, FACE DOWN.` → `THE BACK COMES OFF.` → `SAME HOURS, NOW YOU SEE WHY.`

segments.voice: Year four opens. The first three years asked what happened, and what the text says. This year asks a different kind of question: how does it work? How does a verse become a practice on a Tuesday night? Who decides, and how do they argue? Here is the machinery, in the order this year will open it. First, law. The Mishnah and the Talmud, read plainly: the oral teaching, how it is arranged, how a page of argument turns into a way of living. Second, thought. Maimonides, who tried to show reason and faith working together, and then the mystics of Kabbalah and the Hasidic teachers, who looked for hidden light. Third, the streams. The movements of Jewish life today, each one described in its own terms, with no ranking. Fourth, character. Mussar, the old discipline of working on your traits one at a time: speech, anger, patience. Fifth, the life cycle and the language: birth to mourning, and then the Hebrew letters and roots underneath every word you've met. There's a line in the Psalms that fits a year like this. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Open Thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of Thy law." Notice what it asks for. Not new law. Not a different text. The same Torah, with eyes opened to what was already in it. That's the hope of the year. Nothing you've learned is set aside. The stories stay. The history stays. This year shows the gears that have kept them turning: now, how it works.
screen: `WHAT HAPPENED, THEN HOW IT WORKS.` · `LAW: THE MISHNAH AND THE TALMUD.` · `THOUGHT, STREAMS, CHARACTER.` · `THE LIFE CYCLE AND THE LANGUAGE.` · then, large: `OPEN THOU MINE EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: write one question you want answered this year. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Then let the questions come. Maybe something you've wondered for a long time: why a custom is done the way it is, how a rule got decided, what a Hebrew word really holds. Maybe something smaller. Don't choose the clever one. Choose the one you actually want to know. When the bell ends, write it down somewhere you'll find it again, and leave it there for the year. If you pray, the psalm's words, open Thou mine eyes, are there to borrow. The bell holds the time.
Year four opens. Three years of story, text and history, and now the machinery behind them: law, thought, streams, character, language. Today's word.
Your line: now, how it works. Today, notice one Jewish practice you've learned about and ask yourself the year's question: how does this actually work? Day one thousand sixty-two.

1063.title: Written and oral
1063.hook: tradition holds Moses received a written Torah and an oral teaching that explains it
1063.howItsDone: Rabbinic Judaism reads the written Torah through the oral tradition preserved in the Mishnah and Talmud; practices such as tefillin follow that tradition's explanation of the verses. Some Jewish groups, such as the Karaites, read the written Torah without the rabbinic oral tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday: year four opens, and your line: now, how it works. Did you write down the question you want answered this year? Today, the first gear in the machine. Day one thousand sixty-three.

A man who wants to become a Jew comes to the sage Shammai with a question. How many Torahs do you have? Two, says Shammai. A written Torah and an oral Torah. The man says: the written one I'll believe. The oral one, no. Take me in on the condition that you teach me only the written. Shammai rebukes him and sends him away. So the man goes to Hillel, with the same condition. And Hillel takes him in. This story is in the Talmud, in tractate Shabbat. What Hillel does on the first day of lessons, and then on the second, is today's word.
screen: `HOW MANY TORAHS DO YOU HAVE?` → `TWO.` → `ONLY THE WRITTEN, PLEASE.`

segments.voice: Torah she-be'al peh. The Torah that is on the mouth: the oral Torah. Jewish tradition holds that at Sinai Moses received two things together. The written Torah, the five books on the scroll. And a spoken teaching that explains it, passed from teacher to student. Here's why tradition says the written needs it. Take one verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes." Bind what, exactly? Bind it how? What are frontlets? The scroll doesn't say. The answer Jews live by, small black leather boxes holding handwritten verses, tied on with straps, the tefillin, comes from the oral teaching. Without it, the verse is a beautiful sentence nobody knows how to do. Now back to Hillel and his new student. On the first day, Hillel teaches him the alphabet: alef, bet, gimel, dalet. The next day, he points to the same letters and reads them in the opposite order. The man protests. Yesterday you didn't say it that way! And Hillel answers, in paraphrase: and how did you know yesterday which letter was alef? You trusted me. Trust me about the oral teaching too. Even reading the written Torah, he's saying, already depends on a voice: someone who tells you what the marks on the page are called. In this tradition the scroll and the voice belong together. The written gives the words. The spoken gives them a way to be lived.
screen: `THE TORAH THAT IS ON THE MOUTH.` · `BIND THEM? HOW? THE SCROLL IS SILENT.` · `HILLEL TEACHES THE ALPHABET.` · `WHO TOLD YOU WHICH LETTER WAS ALEF?` · then, large: `THE WRITTEN NEEDS THE SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: explain one rule out loud. Pick any rule you live by: how to fold a flag, how your family sets the table, a rule at work that nobody wrote down. Sit with it for a moment and notice how much of it isn't in any instruction sheet. Then, during the bell, say it out loud, quietly, as if you're teaching someone who has never seen it done. Notice what you have to add that no rulebook ever said. If someone's nearby, explain it to them instead. The bell holds the time.
Torah she-be'al peh. The Torah on the mouth: the spoken teaching that, Jewish tradition holds, came with the written Torah and explains how to live it. Today's word.
Your line: the written needs the spoken. Today, when you read an instruction, notice the part that only makes sense because someone once showed you. Day one thousand sixty-three.

1064.title: Why it was written down
1064.hook: after the revolts against Rome, the oral teachings risked being lost
1064.howItsDone: Jews study the Mishnah by reading it aloud, often with a study partner, and some learn passages by heart; there are groups that study a portion of the Mishnah each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Torah she-be'al peh, the Torah on the mouth, and Hillel teaching the alphabet. Your line: the written needs the spoken. What rule did you explain out loud? Day one thousand sixty-four.

Directions to a good fishing spot, the way an old neighbor gives them. Drive past the church. Turn left at the dead oak. Park where the fence leans, and walk down toward the sound of the water. Perfect directions, as long as the oak is standing and the fence still leans. Then a storm takes the oak. A new owner fixes the fence. And the only person who knew the way moves to another state. The directions haven't changed. The landmarks have. The oral Torah lived like that, in teachers and the places they taught. Then came the wars with Rome, and the landmarks started to fall.
screen: `TURN LEFT AT THE DEAD OAK.` → `THE STORM TAKES THE OAK.` → `THE LANDMARKS START TO FALL.`

segments.voice: Why it was written down. The oral teaching was meant to live in mouths: a teacher saying it, a student saying it back. But after the Temple fell and the revolts against Rome were crushed, Jewish tradition remembers teachers killed and houses of study broken up. A teaching that lives only in people can die with them. So, tradition says, Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered it into the Mishnah. Here's what's surprising about the way it was done. The Mishnah is not a roomy book that explains itself. It's terse. It's tight. It loves lists and patterns. One chapter of Pirkei Avot runs on numbers: with ten sayings the world was created; ten generations from Adam to Noah. That's how you write something you expect people to learn by heart. It was written down so that it could go back into the mouth. That idea is older than the Mishnah. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses is told to write down a song, and in the same breath to teach it to the people and put it in their mouths. Written, so it won't be lost. Spoken, so it stays alive. And the Torah itself warns, in Hebrew, pen tishkach, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen. Now look back at this week. A song of hope, Hatikvah. From generation to generation. What history teaches, and the close of a year of story. Then year four opening, the Torah on the mouth, and today the moment the mouth reached for a pen. Every one of them is about the same worry: how do you keep something alive after the people who knew it are gone?
screen: `A TEACHING THAT LIVES IN PEOPLE.` · `THE WARS WITH ROME; THE LANDMARKS FALL.` · `TERSE, TIGHT, MADE TO BE MEMORIZED.` · `WRITE THE SONG; PUT IT IN THEIR MOUTHS.` · then, large: `WRITE IT BEFORE IT'S LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: write down one thing you only remember. Sit and breathe, and let one thing come to mind that exists nowhere but in your memory. A grandparent's saying. The way to a place. The words of a song someone used to sing you. How a holiday went in the house you grew up in. Stay with it through the bell. Notice the details: the voice, the room, the order things happened. Then, when the bell ends, write it down, short and plain, the way the Mishnah would: so someone else could learn it by heart. The bell holds the time.
Why it was written down. After the wars with Rome, a spoken teaching that could have died with its teachers was set down in the Mishnah, terse enough to memorize. Today's word.

fork.setup: you're a teacher after the wars with Rome. your teachers are gone and your students are scattered. the teaching lives only in memory. what do you do?
options: keep it spoken only, and hope enough people remember.
write a huge book that explains every reason.
gather it into a terse text people can still learn by heart.
fork.reveal: tradition says Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered it into the Mishnah: written so it wouldn't be lost, terse enough to stay on the mouth.

original.note: Hebrew: lest you forget, the Torah's warning in Deuteronomy.

trapdoor: what you thought: once it was written, the oral Torah wasn't oral anymore.
what it means: the teaching was written down so it wouldn't die with its teachers, and written tersely so it could still be learned by heart.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 31:19, write the song and put it in their mouths, and a Mishnah built of lists and patterns, like Avot 5's chains of tens.
